summary: Introduces the Dublin Core, a small set of metadata elements used to describe resources so they can be found. It records the consensus reached on the meaning of each of its 15 elements. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5013.

eli5.summary: Every book in a library has a card listing its title, author and subject. The Dublin Core is a short standard list of such labels that can be used for anything online.

how are dublin core elements organized
what is metadata for resource discovery
subtitle: A simple 15-element standard set for describing and discovering any kind of resource.

tldr.problem: The explosive growth of web resources made it difficult to discover relevant information; existing indexing approaches were poor substitutes for rich resource description.
tldr.mechanism: The Dublin Core Metadata Workshops produced a consensus 15-element set of descriptors organized into three groups: content (what the resource is about), intellectual property (who created it), and instantiation (how to access it).
tldr.outcome: The Dublin Core became the foundation for interoperable resource discovery across digital libraries and the web. RFC 5013 later extended it with qualified elements.

today: RFC 2413 is Informational and has been superseded by RFC 5013, which formalizes the Dublin Core Metadata Element Set version 1.1 and its reference description.

sections.title: The Dublin Core Metadata Standard
sections.content:
RFC 2413 documents the Dublin Core Metadata Element Set, a small set of 15 resource descriptors designed to promote better discovery of electronic resources. The Dublin Core emerged from a series of invitational workshops that began in 1995, bringing together librarians, digital library researchers, and markup experts to establish common semantics for resource description.

The problem being solved was fundamental: as the World Wide Web grew rapidly, full-text indexing became the primary discovery tool, but it was a poor substitute for structured resource description. The Dublin Core provides a minimal, internationally applicable set of elements that can be understood and used across disciplines, systems, and organizations, balancing simplicity with expressiveness.
sections.eli5: As more stuff appeared on the web, people needed a simple way to describe things so they could find them. Dublin Core gives 15 standard labels that anyone can use, no matter what the resource is.

sections.title: Design Principles and Scope
sections.content:
The Dublin Core workshops prioritized six key design goals: simplicity of creation and maintenance, commonly understood semantics, conformance to existing standards, international scope and applicability, extensibility, and interoperability among collections and indexing systems. These goals often work at cross purposes, so much of the workshop effort focused on minimizing tensions among them.

Each Dublin Core element is optional and repeatable, may appear in any order, and can appear with qualifiers that refine its semantics (a subject of future RFCs). Simple indexing tools should be able to ignore qualifiers and still provide basic discovery, while advanced tools can use them for more precise searches. The RFC also recommends adopting case conventions for element labels to support conversion to case-sensitive environments like XML.
sections.eli5: The Dublin Core keeps things simple so anyone can use it, but it is also flexible so more advanced systems can use it in fancy ways. Each element is like a label you can add as many times as you need.

sections.title: The 15 Metadata Elements
sections.content:
The Dublin Core organizes its 15 elements into three groups based on the kind of information they hold. Content elements describe what the resource is about: Title (the name given to the resource), Subject (topic expressed as keywords or phrases), Description (textual summary or abstract), Type (category such as homepage or technical report), Source (information about a resource from which the present resource is derived), Relation (identifiers of related resources), and Coverage (spatial or temporal characteristics).

Intellectual Property elements identify the creators and rights holders: Creator (person or organization responsible for intellectual content), Publisher (entity making the resource available), Contributor (secondary intellectual contributors), and Rights (rights management statement or link). Instantiation elements describe the physical or technical manifestation: Date (creation or availability date in ISO 8601 format), Format (data format and dimensions, identifying software or hardware needed), Identifier (URL, URN, ISBN, or other globally unique identifier), and Language (language of the intellectual content, using RFC 1766 tags).
sections.eli5: The 15 elements fall into three groups: what it is (Title, Subject, Description), who made it (Creator, Publisher), and how to get it (Date, Format, Language). Each element answers a simple question about the resource.

sections.title: Element Semantics and Controlled Vocabularies
sections.content:
Each Dublin Core element has a descriptive name conveying common semantic understanding and a formal single-word label (such as Creator or Rights) for syntactic specification. The RFC recommends controlled vocabularies for several elements to support interoperability. For example, Type should be selected from an enumerated list under development, Format should come from a developing interoperability list, and Relation values should be drawn from an enumerated list of relationship types.

The Date element recommends a profile of ISO 8601 that includes dates in YYYY or YYYY-MM-DD format (for example, 1994-11-05 for November 5, 1994). Language uses RFC 1766 tags. Coverage allows both spatial references (place names or coordinates) and temporal coverage (named periods like 'neolithic' or date/time ranges), though temporal coverage refers to what the resource is about rather than when it was created. Subject and Description elements are intentionally flexible to support keywords, formal classification schemes, and varying levels of detail across domains.
sections.eli5: Each element has a specific meaning. Some have recommended formats (like dates), and some have lists of standard values (like resource types). This helps different systems understand the metadata the same way.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
The Dublin Core is designed for maximum interoperability. Metadata elements may be expressed without qualification (as in this RFC) or with refinements (the subject of future RFCs). The key principle is that simple systems ignoring qualifiers can still discover and understand resources, while sophisticated systems can leverage qualified metadata for more precise retrieval. This approach supports both basic discovery and advanced search within the same standard.

From a security perspective, the Dublin Core element set itself poses no direct risk to computers or networks. However, there is a minimal risk that searchers may obtain incorrect or private information due to careless mapping from rich metadata to the simple 15-element scheme. Organizations using Dublin Core should be aware that element descriptions are intentionally broad to support global interoperability; precise semantics within specific domains should be established through local agreement or community profiles.
sections.eli5: Dublin Core is safe to use because it is just labels describing things. The main thing to watch is that simple systems might not understand nuances in the metadata, so sometimes search results might not be perfect.
